Marcos: No Pax Silica signing in Trump visit

Katrina Domingo,

ABS-CBN News

Published November 18, 2026 11:56 AM PHT

 | 

Updated November 18, 2026 12:28 PM PHT

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his opening speech as he presides over the ASEAN Inter-Parliamentary Assembly at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City on November 15, 2026. Jonathan Cellona, ABS-CBN News
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 1:49
Instaread
MANILA (UPDATED) — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said Wednesday that the Pax Silica initiative would not be signed during US President Donald Trump's visit to the Philippines.

“No, not on this trip. We are not covering that on this trip,” Marcos Jr. said.

“There will be no signing. There is no signing,” US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton also told reporters.

No further details are available as of the moment.

The announcement comes after days of protests were mounted on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in Manila, with farmers, students, indigenous peoples and socio-civic groups urging the Philippine government to reconsider the deal.

ADVERTISEMENT

Among the concerns raised are possible incursions on ancestral domain, the displacement of some indigenous peoples, and the possible shortage of power and water in communities close to the tech hub that would reportedly host artificial intelligence data centers.

The Philippine government has denied these allegations against the multi-billion proposed development in Tarlac, but groups remain wary of the deal.

Bagong Alyansang Makabayan president Renato Reyes Jr. said those opposed to Pax Silica can breathe a sigh of relief.

"This does not mean the agreement won’t be signed in the near future," he said.

He also said the "the biggest victory" of the campaign against Pax Silica is the "high awareness on social issues" it has prompted. 

"We claim as our undeniable victory the massive nationwide discussions and direct actions on the issues of sovereignty, development, the environment and indigenous rights," he said.


 More details to follow.

Skip to next photo


The three-day gathering of 11 leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations came to an end with a festive closing ceremony at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City on Tuesday evening.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., who hailed the summit a success, cited key achievements during the Philippines’ chairship, with discussions focusing on the digital economy, artificial intelligence, maritime security, climate, energy, and sustainability. This year’s meeting also saw the participation of Timor-Leste, represented by Prime Minister Kay Rala Xanana Gusmão, as a full ASEAN member.

Marcos officially turned over the gavel to Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong for the 2027 ASEAN chairship.  Ahead of the official summit, member representatives came together to finalize and sign the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, said to be the first-of-its-kind regional framework that tackles the digital economy, safety, and trade.

The South China Sea Code of Conduct, however, remains unfinished, with only 80 percent of the document finalized given some contentious issues that need to be discussed, according to Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro. 

Officials remain optimistic that the remaining 20 percent will be tackled and finalized at the next ASEAN Summit in Singapore.

Discussions on the second and third day centered on the 29th ASEAN Plus Three, the 21st East Asia Summit, and summits with China, Japan, South Korea, India, Australia and the United Nations.  US President Donald Trump, who arrived early Tuesday evening, met with leaders of the  Quad countries and  co-chaired  the ASEAN-US Summit with Marcos.  

Amid the conduct of the summit, progressive groups held a protest camp in Manila against the visit of Trump and the proposed Pax Silica initiative in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac.

ADVERTISEMENT

Rights groups condemned the arrest last Sunday of protesters—who remain detained at Camp Bagong Diwa—as they attempted to march to Liwasang Bonifacio to join fellow protesters.

Activist groups placed the number of individuals arrested during the Lakbayan Timog Katagalugan at nearly 300, including student activists, representatives of indigenous communities, and even members of the press.

Beijing bolsters South China Sea push with new island runway: analysts

Agence France-Presse

Published November 18, 2026 11:29 AM PHT

 | 

Updated November 18, 2026 04:24 PM PHT

This handout satellite image taken by Planet Labs PBC on October 17, 2026 shows the foundations of a harbour on the disputed Antelope Reef in the Paracel Islands in the South China Sea. Planet Labs PBC/AFP 

China is building a runway on another island in the disputed South China Sea that could significantly strengthen its military footprint in the strategic waterway, according to experts and satellite images seen by AFP.

Beijing claims most of the South China Sea, despite an international ruling that its assertion has no legal basis, and confrontations have occurred regularly with  several Southeast Asian nations over control of the Paracel and Spratly islands.

Both island chains are essentially made up of reefs and outcrops, but analysts say China has been steadily reclaiming land and building infrastructure to gain military control of the sea.

Beijing late last year began large-scale dredging and reclaiming land at Antelope Reef in the Paracel Islands, which are claimed by China, Vietnam and Taiwan, the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and the Lowy Institute said in recent detailed reports, citing satellite images.

ADVERTISEMENT

Lowell Bautista, author of the Lowy Institute report, told AFP that China transformed the reef in 10 months from one of its smallest Paracel outposts into an island that can rival its largest atoll.

The nearly three-kilometre runway on Antelope Reef would be Beijing's second in the Paracels and -- together with infrastructure on the Spratly Islands and on Hainan island -- helps "create an integrated network of runways, harbours and sensors stretching across the sea", Bautista said.

China and Vietnam fought a brief but bloody skirmish over the Paracels in 1974. More than 70 Vietnamese soldiers were killed and China has had de facto control over the islands since then.

The runway is a similar size to an airstrip on the Paracels' Woody Island and three others across the Spratlys, according to CSIS.

Analysts say Antelope -- which is around six kilometres along its northwest-southeast axis -- could become one of China's most important outposts in the South China Sea, potentially helping Beijing limit the access of US and allied naval forces in the event of conflict.

ADVERTISEMENT

China says the development of the Paracel Islands, which it adds have a small resident population of mostly fishers, is for civilian purposes.

A spokesperson for the foreign ministry said in March that China's land reclamation activities there are "necessary construction" for "improving living and working conditions on the islands and growing the local economy".


TRANSPORT PLANES, BOMBERS 

A structure that appears to be a runway is clearly visible in photos taken in September by Earth imaging company Planet Labs.

The images were reviewed as part of a recent report by Japanese intelligence firm Deep Dive and were also seen by AFP.

Deep Dive director Bonji Ohara, a former defence attache in China, said in the report that the structure would be able to handle not just fighter jets but also larger aircraft, including transport planes, aerial refuelling tankers and bombers.

ADVERTISEMENT

The new runway could potentially bring China closer to achieving "full control over the entire South China Sea", he said.

The CSIS has said that Antelope could enhance the reach of Chinese sensing capabilities closer to Vietnam's shores and help expand its military capacity in an area of the northern South China Sea which is close to major shipping lanes.

Antelope Reef's runway is expected to be operational by mid-2027, although other analysts were more cautious about its significance.

The runway and harbour will "add additional capacity and resilience to the facility that enable China's military and paramilitary operations in the South China Sea," Harrison Pretat, deputy director at CSIS's Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative, told AFP.

But "Southeast Asian claimants have still largely maintained access to offshore resources and occupy their own outposts," he said.

ADVERTISEMENT

Majority of issues in South China Sea Code of Conduct 'agreed upon' — Marcos
'Not a failure': PH happy with progress on South China Sea Code of Conduct

LIMITED PUSHBACK 

Nevertheless, Pretat warned that "international attention and pushback... has been far less than might be expected given the scale and significance" of construction, due in part "to distraction from other global crises".

"Regional countries...along with the United States and the international community, should be speaking with a stronger voice against island building and other attempts to permanently alter conditions in disputed areas," he said.

Vietnam in August called construction at Antelope Reef "completely illegal" and demanded "such activities cease immediately".

And in October, Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles said that China's military build-up was creating a "condition of pressure" in Southeast Asia, and urged allies and partners to deepen cooperation.

But Hunter Marston of the Lowy Institute told AFP that "ASEAN (member states) will never be capable of communicating with one voice" due partly to their different views of China.

ADVERTISEMENT

US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the sea, and Filipino and Chinese ships have engaged in repeated confrontations in recent years, some leading to collisions and injuries.

Ohara said that Beijing views the sea as "a sanctuary... where it does not want foreign powers to enter in the event of a contingency" in the region.

"While it will not restrict freedom of navigation in peacetime, if some incident occurs, China intends to prevent not only US naval forces but also those of its allies -- for example, Australian submarines -- from entering," he said.

Trump arrives in Malacañang for state visit

Harlene Delgado,

ABS-CBN News

Published November 18, 2026 11:13 AM PHT

 | 

Updated November 18, 2026 11:53 AM PHT

US President Donald Trump speaks with Philippines' President Ferdinand Marcos Jr during a welcome ceremony at Malacanang Palace in Manila on November 18, 2026. Mandel Ngan, AFP  

MANILA — US President Donald Trump arrived in Malacañang on Wednesday as part of his state visit. 

Trump and the US delegation arrived at 11 a.m. at the Kalayaan Grounds and were regarded with arrival honors. 

He was welcomed by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his son House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, together with Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, Foreign Affairs Secretary Tess Lazaro, Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro, Trade Secretary Cristina Aldeguer-Roque and Philippine envoy Jose Manuel “Babe” Romualdez. 

There, he joined Marcos in the inspection of troops. 

ADVERTISEMENT

As he shook hands with some of Marcos' Cabinet members, Trump was seen talking to Teodoro longer than the other alter egos of the Philippine president.



Marcos also shook hands with US envoy to the Philippines Lee Lipton, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and other American officials.

The two leaders are set to have a bilateral meeting to be followed by a state luncheon before Trump heads to China on Wednesday afternoon for the APEC Summit where he is expected to have a three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump seeks diplomatic gains on Asia tour as Putin arrives in China

Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday for a meeting with the leaders of the so-called Quad countries, including Narendra Modi of India, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese.

Trump's Quad meeting at the 11-member was the security alliance's first since his January 2025 return to power.

Trump tells ASEAN leaders: ‘When there's a problem, you'll call me’ 

While the Quad –- broadly aimed at counterbalancing China's regional influence -- has quietly progressed in deepening coordination, the short time allotted for Tuesday's meeting meant it was unlikely to extend beyond pleasantries, according to analysts.

While Trump was greeted in Manila by a marching band and honor guard on the airport tarmac, elsewhere some 2,000 demonstrators faced off with police, carrying banners reading "Trump out now" and "Reject Pax Silica" -- a reference to a US supply chain initiative that has divided opinion in the Philippines.

Pax Silica signing during Trump visit still up in the air, DFA chief says
